text: Rosa was kneeling by the tomatoes when a cold wind blew across the garden. Her hands were full of soil, so she spoke to the speaker on the porch. "Rain today?" she asked. The assistant understood that she wanted to know if it would rain in her town that day. It checked the forecast and said that light rain would start after lunch and stop by evening. Rosa nodded. A gardener has to learn the weather's habits, and a weekly look at the sky is never enough. "Frost tonight?" she added. The assistant said no, the night would stay above five degrees. Rosa smiled and thanked it. Her grandson had lost a tooth in the dirt last week, and she joked that the garden had kept it. Then she covered the seedlings anyway, just in case the rain came early.

Theo woke up, rubbed his eyes, and reached for his phone. "Hey, show me my new followers from this week," he mumbled. The assistant opened his social media app and began to list the new followers. "No wait, I mean likes, not followers," Theo said. The assistant understood the fix, stopped the list, and read out the likes instead. A huge number had come in overnight, because a friend had shared his photo of the lake from last July. Theo sat up in bed, surprised. The assistant said there were two hundred and forty new likes on that one photo. "Wow," he said. He asked it to turn on notifications for that post only, and the assistant did. Then Theo finally got up to make breakfast.

Nina woke up and remembered the bread dough rising in the closed cupboard, where it had been since last night. Her brother had sent her a recipe card from his trip, and it was written in Italian. She could not read a word of it. "Translate this," she said, holding the card up to her phone's camera. The assistant understood that she wanted the words changed into English. It read the card and told her the dough should rest one more hour, then bake for thirty minutes. "Timer, one hour," she said. The assistant set a timer for one hour. Nina smiled, pulled her blanket back over her legs, and waited. When the timer rang, she turned on the oven, and soon the whole kitchen smelled like warm bread.

Someone wants to know what to pack for a weekend camping trip.
what do i pack for camping
camping list
wat goes in the bag for a night in a tent
I want a packing list for two nights in the hills.
What do people bring when they sleep outdoors?
Tell me what to buy at the pharmacy and what else to put in my bag for the trail.
Is this the correct gear for a cold night by the lake: tent, sleeping bag, stove and torch?
Could you please help me get ready for our camping weekend by listing everything we need?

Max was seven, and he wanted to visit his gran, who lived downstairs from his aunt on the other side of town. He found the tablet and said, "Show me how to get to Gran's house." The assistant already knew the address. It said the bus took twenty minutes and the walk took forty. "Is the bus faster?" Max asked. The assistant said yes, the bus was twice as fast as walking. "How many stops?" Max asked. The assistant said there were six stops, and the last one was right by the park. Max wrote the number six on his hand with a pen so he would not forget it. Then he ran to ask his mum if she would say yes to the trip.

name: party_food_planner
does: Plans a simple menu for a party, such as roast chicken with garlic bread, and tells you how much food to make.
inputs: the number of guests, the kind of party, and any foods a guest cannot eat
people say:
- What should we cook for twelve people on Saturday?
- How much rice do I need if fifteen friends are coming?
- Nothing with nuts, my cousin is allergic.
- Is one cake enough for the whole class?
- I want dinner ideas, and please no dark chocolate this time.
- Help me feed a crowd without spending all day in the kitchen.

Someone wants an alarm to wake them up gently tomorrow morning.
Wake me at six.
No loud beeps, just a soft sound at six thirty.
I have choir practice early, so get me up by half past six.
I don't want to sleep in again, I have a run before work.
Could you set my alarm for seven, but please don't use the harsh ring?
The paid parking starts at eight, so I must be out of bed by seven.
Please make sure I'm awake at dawn without a siren sound.
My ride comes soon, so can you ring a bell at six forty?

Someone wants to be reminded to give an elderly parent the evening medicine.
Pills at eight, please.
Mum always wins the argument about skipping her tablets, so please nudge me tonight.
I keep forgetting Dad's evening dose.
Her humidifier needs water and her tablet is due, so don't let me forget either one.
Make it a fast reminder, Grandpa's medicine is due soon.
I'll be out late, so make sure my phone pings me about the heart pills.
Could you please remind me at eight o'clock to help Grandma take her medicine?
If I don't answer the first time, ask me again.

name: bin_day_helper
does: Tells you which bin to put out on which day for your street, and what goes inside it.
inputs: your street or town, and the kind of waste
people say:
- Which day do the bins go out on the south side?
- Can my watch tell me when to put out the green bin?
- Is it paper day tomorrow?
- Where does a greasy pizza box go?
- I never remember the collection day.
- What can I put in the blue bin?

Dana was packing lunch boxes when she remembered her father. "Remind me to call Dad tomorrow at nine," she said to her phone. A second later she added, "No, make it eight. He leaves for the clinic at ten, and I want to catch him before." The assistant said it had moved the reminder to eight in the morning. Dana's father had needed constant care since his fall last spring, and she often wished she lived closer to him. The assistant then asked if she also wanted a reminder about his pills. Dana said yes, every evening at six. It set both reminders and read them back so she could check. She zipped the lunch boxes into the bags, a little less worried, and ran for the door because the school bus was already honking.

A podcast app keeps your place in every show, so you can stop in the middle of an episode and come back later. People change a few things about it. They change the playback speed when they want a story faster or slower, and they skip ahead thirty seconds when there is an advert. They say things like "go back a bit," "play it faster," or "start the next chapter." On a phone you can drag the line at the bottom to jump to another spot, and a voice assistant does the same when you say "jump to the middle." Some people listen while they cook something crispy in the oven, others while they walk to the store. The app remembers where you left off either way.

Person: Halve it.
Assistant: Happy to. Which recipe do you want me to halve?
Person: The lentil soup. It feeds the whole family, and today I'm only cooking for me.
Assistant: The soup uses four cups of lentils, so half is two cups. Should I halve the other amounts too?
Person: Yes, all of it. Most of the spices too.
Assistant: Done. That is two cups of lentils, three cups of stock and half a spoon of cumin. You can reduce the cooking time by a few minutes.
Person: Thanks. I'm so tired.
Assistant: Rest well after your shift. I can set a timer when you start cooking.

When you order something online, you pick the item, the size and how many you want, and then you choose how it will be delivered. People often change an order before it ships. They say "make it two," "switch to a larger size," or "send it to my office instead." A big box can weigh a lot, so the shop may charge more for delivery, while a small item like an umbrella ships cheaply. If something arrives and looks strange or does not fit, you can send it back. People then ask "how do I return this?" or "when will my money come back?" Keeping the receipt makes everything easier.

name: rain_check_helper
does: Gives a short weather report that tells you if it will rain in your area in the next few hours and when it will start.
inputs: your town, and the hours you want to look at
people say:
- Should I take a coat out with me?
- Will it pour this afternoon?
- Is the sky going to open up before the first bus?
- Is the picnic safe on Sunday?
- Do I need an umbrella?

Someone wants to switch the television to channel twenty-five.
Channel twenty-five, please.
Put on twenty-five.
Go to the channel after twenty-four.
It's a rainy Sunday and I want the old film on twenty-five.
My hands are in the soup pot, stirring, so could you change the channel to twenty-five?
Can you take me to the car show? The one with the horn sound at the start, I think it's twenty-five.
Would you mind switching over to twenty-five? The cooking show is boring.

First aid is the quick help you give someone before a doctor comes. For a small burn, the first step is to hold the skin under cool running water. A gentle stream for about ten minutes is usually right, and people ask "how long should I keep it under the water?" For a cut, you press a clean cloth on it until the bleeding stops. If someone is badly hurt, you call for help straight away. People ask a phone assistant to "call an ambulance," "show me what to do for a bee sting," or "set a ten minute timer." Half the job is staying calm. A first aid kit with working scissors and clean bandages makes everything easier.

Drafting means writing something rough first and fixing it later. A word count tells you how long your piece is, and many people have a limit, like five hundred words for a school essay. Editing means changing words, fixing spelling, and cutting parts that do not help. People say "how many words is this?" "check my spelling," "make this shorter," or "cancel that last change." Even a short note can use a good edit. A letter asking a shop for a refund should be clear and polite, while a cozy story for children can be slower and longer. The goal is always the same: say what you mean in simple words.

Lena had just moved to the city, and she did not know many people. She asked her phone, "Help me find a gift for my neighbour, she turns forty on Saturday." The assistant suggested a plant, some tea and a book. Lena said, "Sorry, not forty, she's turning fifty." The assistant understood the fix and offered a few gifts for someone turning fifty, like a soft scarf. Lena did not want to forget the date, so she asked for a reminder on Friday night. The assistant added it. Her neighbour had been home with a fever that week, so Lena also asked for a short card message. It wrote one line: "Happy birthday, get well soon, and thank you for making me feel welcome." Lena smiled and copied it onto a card.

Someone wants a workout to do today.
Quick workout.
Give me ten minutes of exercise.
I need something easy, and I don't have a gym.
What can I do to stretch and wake up my body?
Help me move a bit, my back is stiff.
Please track my sets while I do push-ups.
Is there a good workout for the shallow end of the pool?
Could you suggest a short routine that I can do at home before dinner, with a rest day built in?

Priya sat at her desk at the office and looked at the calendar on the wall. "How many days until the holiday on the twentieth?" she asked her phone. The assistant counted and said there were nine days left. Then Priya said, "Oh, I meant the twenty-fifth." The assistant counted again and said fourteen days. Priya gave a weak smile and sighed. In the next room, a coworker started to shout about the printer, and someone had left a cup in the sink in the kitchen. Priya laughed. Fourteen days was a long time, so she asked the assistant to remind her one week before. It set the reminder and told her the exact date, so she could stop counting and get back to work.

Person: heat the hot tub for tomorrow at seven
Assistant: Sure. What temperature should it be?
Person: the usual
Assistant: I don't know what your usual is yet. Most people pick thirty-eight degrees. Do you want that?
Person: yes pls. and can you buy more chlorine at the pharmacy
Assistant: Sorry, I can't buy things from a shop. I can put chlorine on your shopping list, though.
Person: ok do that. my sister will draw a smiley on the list lol
Assistant: Done. The hot tub will be at thirty-eight degrees by seven tomorrow, and chlorine is on the list. The total list has four items.

Sam was late for his train, and his coffee machine was still off. He grabbed his phone and said, "Could you please make my coffee strong and with no sugar, because I have a long meeting and I need to stay awake?" The assistant understood that he wanted a strong coffee with no sugar, and it started the machine. While it brewed, Sam read an article on his phone about a private cafe near the station and tried to follow the tips in it. The assistant said the coffee would be ready in two minutes. Sam put on his coat, filled his travel cup, and thanked it. He made the train with one minute to spare.

A washing machine cleans clothes with water and soap, then spins them nearly dry. Most machines have programs: a short wash for a few clothes, a long one for towels, and a cold one for delicate things. People change the temperature, the spin speed and the time. They say "wash it cold," "make it shorter," or "do an extra rinse." A dryer finishes the job, but on a warm day many people hang clothes outside, so they ask about the weather first. Do not pack the drum too full, or the clothes will not get clean. Stains are easier to remove when you treat them early.

A meeting call lets people talk at a set time even when they are in different places. You join with a link, and you can share your screen so others see what you see. An agenda is a short list of what the meeting will cover. People ask for things like "join my ten o'clock call," "share my screen," "mute me," or "send everyone the agenda." Before sharing, close what you do not need so your screen looks clean. In a dark room, the light from a laptop can glow on your face, so turn on a lamp. If you are on the way to work, you can even join from the train station with your phone.

Mr. Okafor sat in his armchair with a book, but the page was hard to read. "It's too dark in here for these old eyes," he said to the speaker. The assistant understood that he wanted more light, and it made the lamp by his chair brighter. "Still a little dim," he said, and it raised the brightness again. Then the assistant asked if he wanted the colour warmer, because the bulb was blue at the moment. He said yes, and the light turned soft and yellow. From the hall he heard the dryer buzz, because the last load of towels was done. He would fold them later. For now, the retired teacher turned the page, happy to read in peace.

Jo was in the kitchen when she spotted the bill for the internet cable on the table. "How much is in my savings account?" she asked the assistant. It said there was four hundred dollars. "Move half of that to my checking account," she said. The assistant understood that she wanted two hundred dollars moved between her own accounts. It did it, then read back the new balances. Her daughter ran in holding a shiny coin from her piggy bank and asked what was going on. Jo laughed and asked, "Is checking more than the cable bill now?" The assistant said yes, checking now had more than the bill, which was eighty dollars. Jo paid it and went back to the dishes.

A clock tells you the time where you are. The world is split into time zones, so when it is noon in one city it may be night in another. People look at a watch or ask a phone, "What time is it in Tokyo?" or "Is it too late to call my sister?" Many people hate waking someone by mistake, so they check first. They also ask a clock to change: "set the clock back an hour" when the seasons change, or "show me two clocks." If you are lucky, your phone updates by itself when you travel to a new place.

A text message is a short note sent from one phone to another. A group chat lets many people read and answer the same conversation. People ask an assistant to write and read texts for them: "text Mum I'm late," "read my new messages," "reply yes," or "tell the group I'll be there at six." It helps to say who the message is for and what it should say. You can ask to change it before it is sent, like "say sorry too." A friend might text to ask if you want to see a show at the theater. Quick replies earn you a name as a good friend.

Ivy woke up to a strange scraping noise outside her window. She was still half asleep, and her room faced the ocean, so she was not used to loud mornings. "The street is making a racket at this hour," she mumbled to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted to know what the noise was. It looked at the neighbourhood news and found a post saying workers were fixing the road early, before the heat of the day. It also said they would finish by noon. Ivy pulled her pillow over her head. The assistant offered to start the fan and play soft rain sounds until then. She said yes, and soon the room felt calm again.

Kai sat in the corner of the library with a pile of notes. "I don't want a long summary, just the due dates," he told his phone. The assistant understood that he wanted only the dates for his assignments. It said the history essay was due Friday and the science quiz was on Monday. "Not the math, I did that already," Kai said. The assistant left the math out. Kai's science project was about iron nails and rust, and he still had to finish the pictures. He asked for a reminder on Thursday evening. The assistant set it. Kai felt calmer, so he rewarded himself with something sweet from his bag and kept studying.

name: fridge_stock_check
does: Tells you what food is running low in your fridge and puts it on your shopping list.
inputs: the name of the food, and how much is left
people say:
- Are we out of milk again?
- Do we still have eggs?
- The juice level is getting low, put it on the list.
- It's silly, but I never remember if we have butter.
- Did I use up the soap for washing dishes?
- What do we need from the shop?

name: screen_time_limit
does: Sets how many minutes a child can use a tablet each day and locks it when the time is up.
inputs: the child's name, the number of minutes, and the day
people say:
- Only one hour of games for Sam today.
- Unlock the tablet after homework, please.
- Give him extra time, his grade went up.
- Maximum two hours on weekends.
- Stop the tablet when it's bedtime.

A smart lock opens and closes your front door without a key. It is for keeping your home safe and for letting the right people in. People ask "lock the door," "is the garage closed?" "who is at the door?" or "let my neighbour in for an hour." When you travel, you can check from far away that everything is shut, which helps if you feel nervous about leaving home. A camera at the door shows who is there, whether it is a delivery person or just a cat climbing a tree. You can also change who has a code, like the person who walks your dog, and remove it later.

Making coffee or tea is a small daily thing, and the details are what people change: how strong, how sweet, how hot, how big. A strong coffee uses more grounds, and a weak tea steeps for less time. People say "a bit less sugar," "make it stronger," "extra milk," or "half a cup." In the morning there is traffic and little time to worry about the details, so a machine started by voice helps a lot. A hungry person might want a smoothie instead, which needs fruit, milk and ice. They say "make it thicker" or "no banana."

When you order food for delivery, a restaurant cooks it and a driver brings it to your door. The app shows how long it will take, and you can add a tip for the driver. People change the order before it is sent: "no onions," "add a drink," or "leave it at the back door." Later they ask "where is my food?" or "how long now?" If it is late, there may be bad traffic or news of a closed road. When it arrives, you unpack the bag and check that everything is there. Some drivers leave a personal note, like "enjoy your dinner."

Ben leaned back in his office chair after a long morning. "Play something calm," he told the speaker, "and wake me with the same playlist tomorrow at seven." The assistant understood both parts. It started a calm playlist and set an alarm for seven the next morning that would play the same songs. Then a coworker walked by and sneezed twice, and Ben's phone buzzed with an urgent message from his boss. "Quieter, please," he said, and the assistant lowered the volume. Ben answered the message, then asked it to bring the music back up a little. The assistant did, and Ben went on with his afternoon.

Someone wants to be reminded when the baby's next feeding is due.
When is the next feed?
I'm at the mall, so tell me when the baby is hungry again and set an alarm for it.
Remind me to make a fresh bottle at three.
Baby eats at four, right? Ping me before.
I'm about to zoom into a work call, so please remind me about the feeding in an hour.
How long since she ate, and when should she eat again?
Could you please let me know a little before the baby's next bottle so I can warm it up?
Nudge me at feeding time, and tell me when the nap starts.

Marta came home hot and tired. "Don't turn the heat on, I want the living room cool," she told the assistant. It understood that she wanted the room cooled and nothing warmer. It tried the air conditioner, but the air conditioner was offline, so it said so. Then it started the fan in the living room instead. Marta saw a loose screw on the fan's stand and tightened it with a coin. Her son wanted to swipe the screen of the tablet to change the speed, but she said, "No, leave it, the speed is fine." The assistant kept it on medium. A cool breeze slowly filled the room, and Marta finally sat down.

Omar had just moved to a new city, and he was nervous about missing things. He said to his phone, "Could you please remind me to call my sister when I get to the train station tomorrow, because she is expecting news about my new job and she will worry if I forget?" The assistant understood that he wanted a reminder tied to a place, not a time. It set the reminder for when he arrived at the train station and told him so. Omar felt relieved. His sister had been waiting for a serious talk about his plans, and he wanted to be sure he called her. In the morning, the phone buzzed right when he walked onto the platform.

Medicine reminders help older people take pills at the right time. A reminder rings at the same hour each day and says which pill to take. People change the time or ask for it to repeat: "remind me every morning at eight," "move it later," or "call my son if I don't answer." If the usual routine breaks, like a day out, they can ask for a different time. For emergencies, a button or a spoken "I need help" can send a call to a nearby family member. Reminders can also be small things, like a neighbour's invitation to tea at four.

Person: Find me a funny film and tell me when it's on tonight.
Assistant: Which cinema should I check?
Person: The Grand, near my restaurant. It's for my gram, she loves comedies.
Assistant: There are two comedies tonight at the Grand, at seven and at nine thirty.
Person: Seven. I'm too busy to type, so please also buy two tickets.
Assistant: Sorry, I can't buy tickets. I can set a reminder to book them, or open the cinema's page.
Person: Remind me at four, then.
Assistant: Done. I'll remind you at four to book two tickets for the seven o'clock comedy.

A robot vacuum is a small, round machine that cleans the floor by itself. It is low enough to slide under a chair, but too low to climb stairs, so it needs a flat floor. People set a cleaning schedule, like every morning at nine, and ask for a different power, such as low, medium or strong. They say "start cleaning," "clean the kitchen only," "stop, I have guests," or "go back to your base." It is a good idea to tidy cables and toys first. When you invite friends over, you might ask it to do a quick extra round before they arrive.

Zoe looked at her calendar and groaned. Too many blue boxes, which meant too many study sessions. "Move football to later, and decrease my study time from two hours to one," she told her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted two changes. It moved football to five in the evening and cut the study block to one hour. "Add more free time on Friday," she said. The assistant made Friday afternoon free. Zoe was meeting some people from her group project on Saturday, and she asked if they were all free. The assistant checked and said four people were free at noon. Zoe sent the time to the group chat and went to find her shoes.

Person: only kitchen
Assistant: I can't turn off a valve by myself, but I can show you where it usually is. Look under the sink for a small tap on the pipe and turn it to the right.
Person: found it. kids brought sand in too, what a mess
Assistant: Good. Turn it all the way off. Should I remind you to call a plumber tomorrow morning?
Person: yes at 8

name: chore_swapper
does: Moves a chore from one child to another and updates the daily chart on the fridge screen.
inputs: the chore, the two children, and the day
people say:
- Sweeping the corner by the door is Mia's job now.
- Can Leo and Ana swap dish duty?
- Put Sam on the trash this week.
- It's Tom's turn to feed the dog.
- Take bed-making off Lily today, she has a cold.

Mrs. Hale sat in her chair with a cup of tea. "Would you be so kind as to turn the robot vacuum on in the living room," she said to the speaker, "because my son and my dad are visiting this afternoon, and the floor is full of crumbs?" The assistant understood that she wanted the robot vacuum to start in the living room. It turned it on and told her it would take about twenty minutes. "Please keep it out of the kitchen," she added. "The stove is hot, and I don't want the machine near it." The assistant told the vacuum to skip the kitchen. Mrs. Hale thanked it and went to set out the cups for her visitors.

Luca stood in his kitchen holding a bottle of wine, getting ready to cook dinner. He thought of his sister, who lived in Sydney. "I wonder if my sister is still up right now," he said to the speaker. The assistant understood that he wanted to know the time in Sydney. It said the local time there was nine in the morning, so she was surely awake. Luca had hoped to call her, but he did not want to miss his cooking, so he asked the assistant to remind him at seven to ring her. It set the reminder. Luca smiled and poured the wine into the pot.

Ana sat on the dirty sofa with a pile of books, and her brain hurt. "I've been studying all day, there must be something fun to see," she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted a film to watch. It found a movie about a girl who loved to travel, showing at the cinema near her house tonight at eight. It also gave the trailer. Ana watched it and liked it. She asked the assistant to save the time, and it added the show to her calendar. She stuffed some candy in her bag, shut her books, and went to wash her face.

name: walk_pace_coach
does: Tells you how fast you are walking or running, and shares a short summary of your trip with a friend.
inputs: the start and end of your walk, and who to send the summary to
people say:
- How fast was I going on that last mile?
- Tweet my distance when I finish.
- Show my pace on the mirror screen in the hall.
- Am I slower than yesterday?
- I only have time for a short route, what's my best loop?

A reminder is a small note that rings at a time or a place. You can say "remind me to water the plants at six" or "remind me when I get home." People use reminders for things they might forget, like wash the cups in the sink or call a friend at seven sharp. They change a reminder when plans move: "push it back an hour," "reset it for tomorrow," or "do it every Monday." Some reminders repeat, and some happen once and then go away. A good reminder says what to do and when, so you know right away.
